about: The look & feel board's history, one step per request. Each step lists the board items it added or changed, as they read at the end of that step. mockups/history_log.py turns this into HISTORY.html; `python3 history_log.py --record <step-id>` appends the changes since the last step from board/items.json.

steps.title: The look & feel board
steps.asked: Set up a digital whiteboard as an HTML page, with text, images and video, to sketch out how the game should look and feel before planning the assets and the build.
changed: A private board page on claude.ai that saves everything to its own database
Nine sections, from Overall vibe to Sound & music, each with a note of starter questions
Notes, images, video, links and color swatches, each of which can be marked Want, Maybe or Avoid
A section in CLAUDE.md with the board's link

items.text:
# How to use this board
- Add notes, images, video clips, links and color swatches with the buttons up top, or drop and paste them anywhere
- Mark anything **Want**, **Maybe** or **Avoid** so we agree on what fits and what doesn't
- Each section has starter questions. Answer them, edit them, delete them, or add sections of your own
- I read this board before we plan, so the more that's here, the closer the game gets to what you picture
items.author: claude

items.text:
# What should it feel like?
- Three words for the mood of the game
- Grim and oppressive, bright and heroic, or something else?
- Which games, films, books or art capture the feeling?
- What should a player say after their first hour?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# How should it look?
- 2D or 3D? Pixel art, hand-painted, low-poly, stylized or realistic?
- Drop in images of the style you want, and mark the ones to avoid
- Add color swatches to sketch the palette
items.author: claude

items.text:
# How do we see the world?
- Isometric, top-down or an angled third-person view?
- How close is the camera? How much of the screen is the hero?
- Fixed angle, or can the player rotate it?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# How should a fight feel?
- Fast and twitchy, or slow and heavy?
- Hordes of weak enemies, or a few tough ones?
- How loud is a hit: screen shake, hit-stop, gore, big damage numbers?
- Clips of combat you love are perfect here
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Who is in it?
- The player: one fixed hero, classes, or build your own?
- What are the enemies: monsters, people, machines, something stranger?
- Bosses: how big and how dramatic?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Where does it take place?
- Setting: dark fantasy, sci-fi, myth, something else?
- Hand-built levels, randomly generated dungeons, or a mix?
- Places you can already picture: caves, cities, ruins, forests?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# What do you collect and grow?
- How much loot drops: a shower or a trickle?
- Skill trees, gear, crafting: which matters most?
- How long should a full playthrough take?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# What is on screen?
- Health and resource bars, a skill bar, a minimap?
- Minimal and clean, or ornate and themed?
- How should the inventory and item tooltips look?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# What does it sound like?
- Music: orchestral, ambient, metal, synth, something else?
- How punchy should hits and spells sound?
- Voice acting, or text only?
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Move with WASD
- W, A, S and D move the character
- Holding two keys walks diagonally
- Assumed: directions follow the screen, so W walks up the screen and A walks left
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Aim with the mouse
- The mouse aims, separately from movement
- You can run one way while aiming and attacking another
- This scheme is often called twin-stick controls
items.author: claude

items.caption: Walking toward the bottom-left while aiming up-right. The character keeps facing the cursor.
items.author: claude

items.text:
# What this means for animation
The character can face one way while moving another, so a forward run alone won't do. It needs movement animations for each direction relative to where it faces: forward, backward, and strafing left and right, blended for the diagonals.

That raises the number of animations we have to make, so it's worth settling early.
items.author: claude

items.text:

- Is there a dodge or dash, and on which key?
- Is moving backward slower than moving forward?
- Should a gamepad work too (left stick moves, right stick aims)?

# What this means for animation
- **Not attacking:** a normal forward walk and run are enough, since the character faces where it goes

items.text:
# Camera control
- Hold the **right mouse button** and move the mouse to orbit the camera around the hero, like in WoW
- Sideways turns the view around the hero
- Up and down changes the angle: from straight down, through the default high view, to low behind the hero
items.author: claude

items.text:
# What a free camera changes
- **WASD follows the camera:** W walks away from the camera, whichever way it faces
- **Right click is taken,** so attacks and skills use left click and the keyboard
- **Low angles show the horizon,** so we need a sky, distant forest and haze to hide the edge of the map
- **Trees must fade** between the camera and the hero at every angle
- **Aiming gets touchy at low angles,** where the ground is seen almost edge-on
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Open camera questions
- Zoom in and out with the mouse wheel?
- How low and how high can the camera go?
- When you let go of the right button, does the camera stay where you left it?
- Should it ever swing back behind the hero by itself?
- Does the mouse cursor hide while you rotate?

steps.title: The whole of Act 1
steps.asked: Look at the whole of Act 1: 10–15 quests and 1–2 hours of play, laid out like act1_layout.png. Past the town comes Storskogen (the fairmeadow), a vast forest with open plains, thick forest, raised ground and hollows, all with slopes you can walk. Make top-down blueprints of the act and screenshots from different zones at different camera angles.
changed: The act traced from your sketch at about 1.2 m per unit: seven areas and about 1.2 km² to walk
Storskogen: open meadows, a thicket, an esker ridge, a lookout hill and a kettle-hole hollow, and no slope in the act steeper than 20°
12 quests (7 main, 5 side): about 80 minutes for the story, 1 h 55 min for everything
Two blueprints and ten screenshots, A–J, all made from the same world data

items.text:
# Act 1 at a glance
- Seven areas traced from your act1_layout.png, at about 1.2 m per sketch unit
- **Tallmo** (town) opens onto **Storskogen**, the hub
- From Storskogen: **Härddalen** to the north-east, **Gamla gården** to the east, **Dimskogen** to the north-west
- Dimskogen leads down to **Dimmyren**, then a winding path west to **Ödeskogen**, where the act ends
- About 1.2 km² to walk; Storskogen alone is about 720 × 650 m
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Zone names (suggestions)
- **Tallmo**: the town
- **Storskogen**: the fairmeadow
- **Härddalen**: Hearthvale
- **Gamla gården**: the Old Courtyard
- **Dimskogen**: the Misty Woods
- **Dimmyren**: the Misty Swamp
- **Ödeskogen**: the Forsaken Forest
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Main story (placeholder)
- **1 Vägen ut:** clear the road to the crossroads
- **4 Vårdkasen:** light the beacon on the lookout hill
- **5 Den kalla härden:** find the survivors of the burned farm
- **8 Förvaltarens brev:** the steward's letter points to the fog
- **9 När dimman kommer:** follow the wisps into Dimskogen

- **Rocks:** chunky, with uneven faces of mixed shapes and sizes, not lots of small triangles

items.text:
# Worn paths
Paths are worn into the grass by feet, so they no longer end in a hard line:
- **Edges:** the grass thins out in ragged clumps toward the path, and the grass along it is drier and trampled

- **Props:** low grass tufts and pebbles along the edges break up the outline
- **Also:** roads now show through meadows and the town, where the meadow grass used to cover them, and the needle litter under trees fades out instead of ending in a zigzag

With the gravel showing, the paths read a little greyer. The mix of dirt and gravel is easy to tune.

steps.title: Shadows, ground detail and path colours
steps.section: Play demo: path colours and speed
steps.asked: Shadow distance makes a noticeable difference, but lowering it made many shadows near the player disappear, and the shadows add a lot of immersion: save performance by making them less detailed instead of removing them. Removing the ground details made a huge difference: give different degrees of ground detail, without removing it altogether. And give more versions of the path colour and ground details: the current one feels too much like sand; a little more colour contrast, without going too dark brown, with themes from darker brown to sandy that fit a Swedish forest
changed: Shadow distance: by default it now fits the view, reaching just past the top of the screen, so the shadows round the hero never go; it is 2 ms faster than the fixed 70 m
Less detailed shadows to try in the performance panel: resolution from 4096 to 512, softness and cascades. At 1024 every shadow stays, softer, 4.8 ms faster
The ground shader at four levels of detail, each compiled on its own: Medium looks almost the same as High and is 4.6 ms faster, Low 4.7, Off 5.0
Cheaper ground detail at every level: a faster hash for the noise, simpler stone outlines below High, and a cheaper test for the fallen leaves
Seven path colour themes, from dark forest soil to light sand, most with stones that stand out from the dirt. P cycles through them, and the panel lists them
Ambient occlusion levels in the panel: off saves 6.1 ms, very low 0.6
Trees fading near the camera now go in patches instead of a dither of single pixels, which the ambient occlusion turned into black specks

items.author: claude

items.text:
# Path colours and speed
You asked for:
- shadows that stay, only less detailed, instead of a shorter shadow distance
- levels of ground detail between all and none
- path colours with more contrast than the light tan, from darker brown to sandy, that fit a Swedish forest

In the demo, **P** cycles through the seven path colours, and **F2** opens the performance panel with the new shadow and ground options.

Each colour below shows the default camera on the left and a forest close-up on the right. Mark the ones you like with Want, Maybe or Avoid.
items.author: claude

items.caption: Forest soil: dark, packed forest soil with grey-brown stones and more fallen leaves.
items.author: claude

items.caption: Brown earth: medium brown earth with pale, sandy stones.
items.author: claude

items.caption: Iron soil: warm, rusty brown soil, as where the ground is rich in iron, with grey granite stones.
items.author: claude

items.caption: Granite gravel: a grey-beige track of crushed granite, grey and pink, with more stones.
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Shadows
**Why they went:** the shadow distance counts from the camera, not the hero, and the camera is 20 m from the hero. Set below about 35 m, it cuts shadows at the top of the screen; below about 25 m, the ones round the hero go.

**Now:** by default the distance fits the view, reaching just past the top of the screen, so it never cuts the shadows you can see. That is 2 ms faster than the old fixed 70 m.

**Less detailed, not fewer:**
- Shadow resolution 1024: softer edges, every shadow kept, 4.8 ms faster
- 512: blurrier, and gaps start to show
- Tree shadows from the far trees: simpler crowns, 4 ms faster

Times are per frame on this laptop's graphics card.
items.author: claude

items.caption: Esker sand: pale sand and gravel, as on the eskers, with grey-brown pebbles.
items.author: claude

items.caption: Sandy, mixed stones: the light tan paths' sandy dirt, with stones of mixed browns and greys standing out from it.
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Ground details
The ground shader comes in four levels now, each compiled on its own, so a lower level doesn't pay for what it skips:
- **High:** everything, as before
- **Medium:** no flat stones, grit or bumps, and simpler stone outlines. It looks almost the same, and is 4.6 ms faster
- **Low:** the small stones and the leaves only, 4.7 ms faster
- **Off:** 5.0 ms faster

I suggest Medium: nearly all of Off's speed, and the paths keep their gravel and leaves.

found: The shadow distance counts from the camera, which is 20 m from the hero, so below about 25 m the shadows round the hero go
Nearly all of the ground's cost is in what only High draws: the bumps, the exact, wavy stone outlines, the flat stones and the grit
The black specks left by trees fading near the camera came from the ambient occlusion: worked out at half resolution, it blackens the ground between single dithered pixels
Under the forest's blue ambient light, grey paths read blue-grey, so the grey themes needed warmer stones

steps.asked: Of the path colours, a mix of forest soil and brown earth is the favourite. The path still looks a bit uniform, even with its uneven edges: spread the wear out more, so it's less clear exactly where the path goes, perhaps using the mix of forest soil and brown earth. Is the play demo held at 60 fps? Lowering the ground detail never takes it past 60: uncap the frame rate, or better, add a slider to set it. And instead of the round see-through hole, make any tree in the line of sight from the camera to the player invisible altogether, so the area round the player is easier to see through the trees
changed: A new path colour theme, Forest earth: patches of dark forest soil a metre or two across in medium brown earth, more of it toward the edges, with grey-brown and pale stones. The demo starts with it

Path wear spread, in the performance panel: the ground bake now keeps each spot's distance from the trail's centre line, so the game works out the wear itself. At 1, the new default, the trampled grass, bare patches and stray stones reach about twice as far into the grass and break up in patches; at 0 the wear is the mockups'

Physics interpolation keeps the hero's movement smooth above the physics' 60 steps a second

items.text:
# Paths
- **Forest earth** is a new colour theme, and the demo starts with it: patches of dark forest soil a metre or two across in medium brown earth, with more soil toward the edges. P still cycles through the others
- **Path wear spread** in the F2 panel sets how far the wear reaches: 0 as before, 1 the furthest and the new default. The trampled grass, bare patches and stray stones reach about twice as far into the grass, and break up in patches

# Trees in the way
- A tree between the camera and the hero, or the ground within 3 m of the hero, fades out whole in a fifth of a second, and comes back once it's out of the way. Its shadow stays
- From the default high camera that's rare; it matters when you orbit low
- In the F2 panel: **Trees in the way** (Hide or Keep), and how much ground round the hero to keep clear, 0 to 8 m
- Hidden trees aren't drawn, so hiding them costs the graphics card nothing; finding them takes 0.1 to 0.3 ms a frame

# Frame rate
- VSync held it at 60, the screen's refresh rate. VSync now starts off, with no limit, so it goes as high as the graphics card manages
- **Frame rate limit** in the F2 panel: 30 to 250 fps, or none at the slider's right end
- At the start, on this laptop: 54 fps with the default settings, 69 with Medium ground details, 77 without shadows, 97 with the old trees. Walking the trail averages 68
- The hero still moves 60 times a second and is drawn smoothly in between, so walking stays smooth at any frame rate

found: The frame rate never passed 60 because VSync, on by default, holds it to the screen's refresh rate

The mockups' wear was baked into the ground masks with its falloff fixed at about two half-widths from a path's centre, so to spread it further the bake had to keep the distance from the centre instead
Each tree's fade is a value per drawn instance, and Godot's default buffer for those holds only about 4,000 instances; with both tree sets the demo has about 19,000, so the buffer is now 8 MB

items.title: Play demo: trees go once they're in the way
items.author: claude

items.text:
# Trees go once they're in the way
You said the trees disappeared a bit early, even before the hero reached them, and should only go once some part of them is between the camera and the hero.

Now:
- A tree goes once one of its leaf cards, branches or its trunk is on a line from the camera to the hero, tested against the tree's own shape as it's drawn
- Trees the hero walks towards stay until they're between the hero and the camera
- No more clearing round the hero: the 3 m ring is gone, and so is the mockups' fade of the trees near a high camera. Both can be turned back on in F2 ("clear round the hero", "Fade trees near camera")
- Only what the camera is about to touch, within about 2.5 m of it, still fades
items.author: claude

items.caption: Walking up to the Scots pine and past it, from the default camera. Before (top) it went 5 m early, with everything round the hero; now (bottom) it stays until the hero is behind it.
items.author: claude

items.text:
# How early, before and now
Walking up to a tree from the default camera, it went:
- **Scots pine:** 5 m before its trunk; now 1.5 m, as its branches reach the hero
- **Norway spruce:** 7 m before; now 2.5 m, as its low branches reach over the hero

At 24 random spots and camera angles, trees covered at most 1% of the hero. A few went up to a metre early, from the see-through parts of their leaf cards.

**Speed:** the trees round the hero are drawn now, so the start runs at 51 fps instead of 54; walking the trail averages 65.

wip.caption: The fade of the trees near a high camera, stopped short of the hero (left) or off (right): the same at the default camera, cleaner low down, but slower, so it's off

found: The 3 m ring round the hero, and the fade of the trees near a high camera, which reached past the hero, made trees go 3 to 7 m before they were in the way
Testing against the trimmed leaf cards could miss needles that show; the square cards always contain them, so the test uses those, whichever are drawn
Seen from above, lines to an upright slice through the hero miss what covers its footprint, so the points lie on a plane facing the camera
Trees half faded near the camera cost more to draw than whole ones, so stopping that fade short of the hero made the start 2 ms slower; it's off now
Working out a tree's shape the first time it came near the camera stalled a frame; it's done as the trees load
At 24 random spots and camera angles, trees covered at most 1% of the hero; a few went up to a metre early, from the see-through parts of their leaf cards
